editorial.headline: Wholesale Musical Instruments, and Bali’s Closed PMA Door
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale musical-instrument trade is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent moratorium makes PMA registration unavailable on the island.
editorial.body:
KBLI 46493 concerns wholesale trade in a broad range of musical instruments. Its stated scope includes traditional instruments such as kecapi, bamboo flutes, calung, angklung, kolintang, gamelan, rebab, rebana, tifa and sasando. It also reaches modern instruments including flutes, saxophones, harmonicas, trombones, guitars, mandolins, ukuleles, harps, basses, violins, cellos, pianos, organs, drums and tuning forks. The range is explicit: traditional and modern instruments sit together within one wholesale activity.

The recorded scale access is equally direct. Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar are all open to this activity. That gives the classification a place for businesses at each of the four recorded scales, without changing the thing being registered: wholesale trade in the instruments within its stated scope. The activity description answers what is traded; the scale listing establishes that it is open across the recorded micro, small, medium and large categories.

At national level, the PMA picture is unambiguous. The activity is marked TERBUKA and its maximum foreign ownership is 100 per cent. In other words, the national foreign-ownership ceiling permits full foreign ownership for this activity, with the record citing Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021 as its PMA source. This is a national position for this one wholesale activity, and its significance lies in the clarity of that ceiling rather than in any assumed provincial outcome.

That provincial outcome is decisive in Bali. A PMA company cannot register this activity in Bali today. Its Bali status is BLOCCATO_CLASSE_RISCHIO: at the Besar scale, OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope, and the record identifies the Bali moratorium as the reason for the block. That moratorium is island-wide and permanent, blocking all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities from PMA registration; the stated Bali reason identifies it in May 2026. The national 100 per cent ceiling remains the national fact, but it does not remove the Bali block.
